summary:
Dancing with StARs is an interactive application that helps people explore changes in Earth’s surface using radar data from the NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) mission.

Users can search for a location, select an area on a map, and choose a time interval. The application searches for compatible NISAR observations, compares two radar images, and displays areas where the radar signal may have changed. Users can explore the mapped regions and view details such as their estimated area and observation dates.

Our prototype uses a machine learning model trained on NISAR data from selected European regions. It brings together satellite data, automated analysis, and an interactive map to make radar observations easier to explore and communicate.

Changes in radar signals can be related to vegetation, water, soil moisture, or human activity. The application highlights possible changes for further investigation; it does not determine their cause or automatically identify specific events. Results require validation using additional data.
details:
Dancing with StARs is an interactive Earth observation application that helps users explore possible surface changes using NISAR synthetic aperture radar (SAR) data.

The user searches for a location, draws an area of interest on an interactive globe, and selects a date interval. The application searches the Alaska Satellite Facility catalogue for compatible NISAR Level 2 GCOV observations. When a suitable pair is available, the observations are downloaded, prepared for analysis, and compared using our trained change-detection model.

The results are displayed on the map as highlighted regions. Users can select a region to see its estimated mapped area and the dates of the two observations. This gives users a more intuitive way to explore radar data without having to process satellite products manually.

We trained a Siamese U-Net model using NISAR observations from selected European regions. Our prototype uses HH and HV polarization channels and pseudo-labels to learn patterns of change. The model was exported to ONNX for use in the application.

The interface was built with React, TypeScript, and CesiumJS. The backend uses Rust and Python, with FastAPI, ONNX Runtime, and geospatial libraries to retrieve and process the data. Google Colab was used for model training.

Our goal is to make satellite radar observations more accessible to students, educators, and people interested in environmental change. The highlighted areas represent possible changes in radar response, which can be influenced by vegetation, water, soil moisture, or human activity. The current prototype does not determine the cause or classify specific events. Its results require further validation against reference data before they can support scientific or operational decisions.

The availability of compatible NISAR observations depends on the selected location and dates. The model was trained on selected European regions, so its performance in other areas has not been established.
